label: Chapter XI
title: The Nine Grounds
paragraphs: Master Sun said: The rule in war is this. There is scattering ground, light ground, contested ground, meeting ground, crossroads ground, heavy ground, rough ground, hemmed-in ground and death ground.

When a prince fights on his own land, it is scattering ground. When he has entered another's land, but not deeply, it is light ground. Ground that is an advantage to us if we take it and an advantage to him if he takes it is contested ground.
Ground where we can go and he can come is meeting ground. Ground where the lands of three princes join, so that whoever gets there first wins the multitudes of the world, is crossroads ground.

When he has entered deep into another's land, with many walled cities and towns at his back, it is heavy ground. Mountains and forests, steep and blocked places, marshes and swamps, all roads that are hard to travel, are rough ground.

Ground where the way in is narrow and the way back is roundabout, where his few can strike our many, is hemmed-in ground. Ground where you survive if you fight at once and perish if you do not is death ground.

That is why on scattering ground you do not fight. On light ground, do not stop. On contested ground, do not attack. On meeting ground, do not let yourself be cut off. On crossroads ground, join with your allies. On heavy ground, plunder. On rough ground, keep moving. On hemmed-in ground, use strategy. On death ground, fight.

Those who were called skilled in war in ancient times could keep the enemy's front and rear from reaching each other, his many and his few from relying on each other, his noble and his common men from rescuing each other, those above and those below from holding together. His soldiers were scattered and could not be gathered; his troops, when they came together, could not be put in order.
Move when it is to your advantage; when it is not, stay where you are.
May I ask: "If the enemy is many and in good order and about to come, how do we wait for him?" I say: "First seize what he loves, and he will listen."
So it is the nature of war that speed rules. Take the enemy before he is ready, go by roads he does not expect, and attack where he is not on guard.
The way of an invader is this. Go in deep and the men hold together, and the defender cannot overcome you. Plunder the rich fields and the whole army has enough to eat.
Look after the men with care and do not tire them. Gather their spirit and store up their strength. Move the troops and lay your plans so that no one can fathom them.
Throw them where there is nowhere to go, and they will die before they run. If they will die, what can they not do? Officers and men will give all their strength.
Soldiers sunk deep in danger have no fear. With nowhere to go they stand firm. Deep in enemy land they hold together. With no choice left, they fight.
That is why such troops are watchful without being drilled, do what is wanted without being asked, are loyal without being bound, and can be trusted without being ordered.
Forbid omens and do away with doubts, and until death they will think of going nowhere.
If our men have no wealth to spare, it is not because they dislike goods. If they have no life to spare, it is not because they dislike long years.

On the day the order goes out, the tears of the men who are sitting soak their collars, and the tears of those lying down run across their cheeks. But throw them where there is nowhere to go, and they have the courage of Chu and Kuei.

So one skilled in war is like the shuai-jan. The shuai-jan is a snake of Mount Ch'ang. Strike its head and the tail comes at you. Strike its tail and the head comes at you. Strike its middle and head and tail both come at you.

May I ask: "Can an army be made like the shuai-jan?" I say: "It can. The men of Wu and the men of Yüeh hate each other. Yet when they are crossing a river in the same boat and meet a storm, they help each other like the left hand and the right."

That is why tying the horses together and burying the chariot wheels is not enough to rely on. To level their courage so that they are as one is the way of command. To get the best from both the hard and the soft is the pattern of the ground.
So one skilled in war leads the army as if he led one man by the hand. They have no choice.
The business of the general is to be still and so unreadable, upright and so in order.

He can dull the ears and eyes of his officers and men and keep them without knowledge. He changes his arrangements and alters his plans, so that no one understands. He shifts his camp and takes roundabout roads, so that no one can work out what he intends.

When the commander brings them to the appointed hour, it is like climbing a height and kicking away the ladder. The commander leads them deep into the land of the princes and releases the trigger. He burns the boats and breaks the cooking pots. He drives them like a flock of sheep, driven this way and driven that way, and none knows where they are going.
To gather the whole army and throw it into danger: this is called the business of the general.
The changes of the nine grounds, the advantages of drawing in and stretching out, the pattern of human feeling: these must be examined.

The way of an invader is this. Deep in, the men hold together; shallow in, they scatter. When you leave your own state and take the army across the border, it is cut-off ground. Where roads lead out on all four sides, it is crossroads ground. When you have gone in deep, it is heavy ground. When you have gone in a little way, it is light ground. Where there are strongholds behind and a narrow way ahead, it is hemmed-in ground. Where there is nowhere to go, it is death ground.

That is why on scattering ground I would make the men of one purpose. On light ground I would keep them close together. On contested ground I would hurry up my rear. On meeting ground I would see to my defenses. On crossroads ground I would make my alliances firm. On heavy ground I would keep the food coming. On rough ground I would press on along the road. On hemmed-in ground I would block the gap. On death ground I would show them that they will not live.
For it is the nature of soldiers to resist when surrounded, to fight when there is no choice, and to follow when things have gone past all limit.

That is why whoever does not know the plans of the other princes cannot make alliances beforehand. Whoever does not know the form of the mountains and forests, the steep and blocked places, the marshes and swamps, cannot march an army. Whoever does not use local guides cannot get the advantage of the ground.
Whoever does not know one of these four or five does not have the army of an overlord.
When the army of an overlord attacks a great state, that state cannot gather its forces. When its power bears down on the enemy, his allies cannot join him.

That is why the overlord does not compete for the alliances of the world or build up the power of others in the world. He follows his own purposes, his power bears down on the enemy, and so the enemy's cities can be taken and his state overthrown.
Give rewards outside the rules. Post orders outside the regulations. Drive the whole army as if you were directing one man.
Drive them with the task; do not tell them the reasons. Drive them with the advantage; do not tell them the harm.
Throw them onto ground where they must perish, and they will survive. Sink them in death ground, and they will live. Only when the men are sunk in harm can they decide victory and defeat.

So the business of war lies in pretending to go along with the enemy's intentions. Bring your force against him in one direction, and from a thousand li away you kill his general. This is called accomplishing the thing by skill.
That is why, on the day war is decided, you close the passes, break the tallies and let no envoys through. In the temple hall you press the matter hard, to settle the plan.
When the enemy opens his door, be sure to go in at once. Get first to what he loves, and keep your hour hidden from him. Walk the marked line and follow the enemy, until the battle is decided.
That is why at first you are like a maiden, and the enemy opens his door. Afterward you are like a hare let loose, and the enemy is too late to shut you out.

divergences.locus: the title, and XI.1–14, the nine grounds
divergences.phrase: scattering ground, light ground, contested ground, meeting ground, crossroads ground, heavy ground, rough ground, hemmed-in ground and death ground
divergences.older: Giles (1910): title "The Nine Situations"; "(1) Dispersive ground; (2) facile ground; (3) contentious ground; (4) open ground; (5) ground of intersecting highways; (6) serious ground; (7) difficult ground; (8) hemmed-in ground; (9) desperate ground."
divergences.lectio: There is scattering ground, light ground, contested ground, meeting ground, crossroads ground, heavy ground, rough ground, hemmed-in ground and death ground.
divergences.note: The title is 九地, "nine grounds", and each name is one word before 地. 散 is "scatter": at home the men are near their families and slip away. 輕 and 重 are "light" and "heavy", a shallow and a deep entry into enemy land, and the pair is kept as a pair. 交 is where two sides' roads meet; "open" is used in this edition for the first terrain of Chapter X, which has the same definition but a different name. 衢 is a crossroads. 圮 is ruined, broken country. 死地 is "death ground"; Giles's "desperate" softens the word. The same names are used for the five grounds listed in Chapter VIII.

divergences.phrase: the courage of Chu and Kuei
divergences.older: Giles (1910): "But let them once be brought to bay, and they will display the courage of a Chu or a Kuei."
divergences.lectio: But throw them where there is nowhere to go, and they have the courage of Chu and Kuei.
divergences.note: 諸、劌之勇. The text gives one syllable of each name and so does the English. Chu is Chuan Chu, who killed King Liao of Wu in 515 BC with a dagger hidden in a cooked fish and was cut down on the spot. Kuei is Ts'ao Kuei of Lu, who in 681 BC held a dagger to Duke Huan of Ch'i at a treaty meeting and made him give back the land Lu had lost. Both were bywords for the courage of a man with nothing left to lose. The first clause repeats 投之無所往 from earlier in the chapter and is given the same English.

divergences.phrase: When the commander brings them to the appointed hour
divergences.older: Giles (1910): "At the critical moment, the leader of an army acts like one who has climbed up a height and then kicks away the ladder behind him. He carries his men deep into hostile territory before he shows his hand."
divergences.lectio: When the commander brings them to the appointed hour, it is like climbing a height and kicking away the ladder. The commander leads them deep into the land of the princes and releases the trigger.
divergences.note: 帥與之期，如登高而去其梯；帥與之深入諸侯之地，而發其機. 期 is an appointed time: the moment the general has fixed for the fight and told no one. 發其機 is "releases the trigger", the crossbow image of Chapter V, where momentum is the drawn bow and timing the release; Giles's "shows his hand" changes the picture. "He burns the boats and breaks the cooking pots" (焚舟破釜) stands in the cached text and in Giles's, but is missing from some old editions and may be a later addition.

divergences.phrase: one of these four or five
divergences.older: Giles (1910): "To be ignorant of any one of the following four or five principles does not befit a warlike prince."
divergences.lectio: Whoever does not know one of these four or five does not have the army of an overlord.
divergences.note: 四五者，不知一，非霸王之兵也. Nobody knows what "the four or five" are. Giles pointed the phrase forward. Ts'ao Ts'ao took it as "the four and the five", that is, the nine grounds, and some editors emend to 此三者, "these three", meaning the three sentences just repeated from Chapter VII. We translate the words as they stand and point them back at what has just been said. 霸王 is a ruler strong enough to command the other princes; "overlord" says that without Giles's "warlike".

divergences.phrase: pretending to go along with the enemy's intentions … Walk the marked line and follow the enemy
divergences.older: Giles (1910): "Success in warfare is gained by carefully accommodating ourselves to the enemy's purpose." and "Walk in the path defined by rule, and accommodate yourself to the enemy until you can fight a decisive battle."
divergences.lectio: So the business of war lies in pretending to go along with the enemy's intentions.
divergences.note: In XI.60 the cached text reads 佯順敵之意, "feigning to follow the enemy's intent"; Giles's text had 順詳, which he took as "carefully accommodating". The pretending fits what follows: the enemy is led on, then struck from one direction. In XI.67 踐墨 is literally "tread the ink line", the line a carpenter snaps onto wood to cut by. It has been explained as keeping to the rules of war, as keeping to one's plan in silence, and, with a different first character (剗), as throwing the rules away. We keep the image and do not decide.
